title: The integer borrow has exactly two outcomes, and each is witnessed by a natural
statement: For any property P of integers and any naturals m and n: if P holds of ofNat i whenever n + i = m, and P holds of negSucc i whenever m + (i+1) = n, then P holds of the normalized difference of m and n.

formal.statement: theorem Int.subNatNat_elim : ((x0 : ((x0 : Int) -> Prop)) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat) -> ((x3 : ((x3 : AxNat) -> ((x4 : Eq.{1} AxNat (AxNat.add x2 x3) x1) -> x0 (Int.ofNat x3)))) -> ((x4 : ((x4 : AxNat) -> ((x5 : Eq.{1} AxNat (AxNat.add x1 (AxNat.succ x4)) x2) -> x0 (Int.negSucc x4)))) -> x0 (Int.subNatNat x1 x2))))))

notes: The case-analysis principle the four blocked laws were missing. Its content is that `Int.subNatNat m n` is `Int.ofNat i` exactly when `m` dominates by `i`, and `Int.negSucc j` exactly when `n` dominates by `j+1` -- and that those two cases are exhaustive, which is `Nat.le_total` turned into explicit differences by `Nat.le_dest`. The `m <= n` half must still split its difference, because a difference of `0` is the NON-borrowing case and has to be routed to the first branch. Stating the second outcome as `negSucc j` rather than `negOfNat k` is deliberate: it makes the two branches disjoint, so a caller learns the sign and not merely the magnitude. `formal.statement` is `Kernel::render_lean` of the admitted type, verbatim from `int_theorem_inventory`.
